content: The Steering Group, which included technical experts, guideline methodologists, and systematic review teams, oversaw the development of the guideline. This included evidence retrieval and synthesis, preparation of evidence-to-decision tables using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) and DECIDE (Developing and Evaluating Communication strategies to support Informed Decisions and practice based on Evidence) frameworks, and the organization of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting. The Steering Group also drafted the recommendations, finalized the guideline document, and managed its publication and dissemination. Members of the Steering Group are listed in Annex 2. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was composed of 20 external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions. This diverse group included individuals with expertise in research, guideline development, health policy, clinical care, and reproductive health programs. It also included representatives from organizations advocating for women’s rights, particularly the right to respectful and quality care during childbirth. Biographies of GDG members were made publicly available for review and comments before the September 2017 GDG meeting. Selected GDG members participated in a scoping meeting in April 2016 to define the guideline’s scope, prioritize questions, and provide input on evidence summaries and decision tables. The GDG formulated and approved the final guideline document before its submission to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. Members of the GDG are listed in Annex 2. The External Review Group (ERG) consisted of six technical experts and stakeholders with an interest in evidence-based maternal and newborn care. The group was selected based on criteria such as geographic balance, gender representation, and the absence of conflicts of interest. The ERG peer-reviewed the final guideline document for factual accuracy, clarity, contextual relevance, and implementation implications. They also assessed whether the decision-making processes incorporated relevant contextual values and perspectives of affected individuals, including pregnant women, their families, healthcare professionals, and policymakers. The ERG did not alter the recommendations formulated by the GDG. Members of the ERG are listed in Annex 2. The Technical Working Group (TWG) included guideline methodologists and systematic review teams. Two health system researchers, who were also editors of the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) group, served as guideline methodologists. Evidence on the effectiveness of non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections was derived from a Cochrane review maintained by the EPOC group. The methodologists collaborated with review authors and the WHO Steering Group to update the review and prepare GRADE evidence tables. They also synthesized case studies to identify contextual factors likely to influence the adoption and scale-up of cesarean-related interventions. Evidence on barriers and facilitators to non-clinical interventions was derived from three systematic reviews of qualitative studies. The preparation of these reviews, including GRADE and CERQual (Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research) assessments, was commissioned from researchers at the University of Central Lancashire, United Kingdom. The WHO Steering Group commissioned a scoping review in 2015 to identify interventions aimed at reducing cesarean rates. This review included 11 systematic reviews published between 2001 and January 2016, covering 99 unique studies conducted in 32 countries, mostly high-income. These studies examined 151 intervention components grouped into four domains: A scoping meeting held in Geneva in April 2016 identified priority questions and defined the guideline’s scope in terms of key background and foreground questions. Background questions provided contextual information for the recommendations, while foreground questions guided the evidence review. The focus of this guideline is on non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. Preparatory work was organized into three work streams: updating Cochrane reviews on intervention effectiveness and safety, synthesizing qualitative evidence on barriers and facilitators, and analyzing implementation considerations. Evidence was derived from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials, interrupted time series studies, and cohort studies. Qualitative evidence was synthesized using meta-ethnography, which involves comparing and contrasting findings across studies. The DECIDE framework was used to guide the formulation of recommendations. This framework considers six domains: effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Judgments were made on the impact of interventions against these domains to inform guideline recommendations. The strength of recommendations was influenced by the certainty of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, and the values and preferences of affected individuals. Resource implications, including cost-effectiveness, were also evaluated. Strong recommendations were made when benefits clearly outweighed harms or when resource implications were advantageous, while conditional recommendations were made in cases of uncertainty. The guideline emphasizes the importance of non-clinical interventions in reducing unnecessary cesarean sections and provides evidence-based recommendations to support their implementation.
